parakeet: In this context, we could argue that no weapon ever forged is as dangerous as a conviction. While a sword can kill an individual, a belief can mobilize an entire generation to see their neighbors as obstacles to a higher purpose. Even our biological survival is tethered to the accuracy of our beliefs, as seen in the evolution of medicine. For centuries, the medical world operated under the belief in the four humors and miasma, the idea that disease was caused by bad air or internal imbalances of fluid. These beliefs weren't just wrong, they were deadly because they prevented the discovery of actual pathogens. It was only when these beliefs shifted toward germ theory that we begin to save billions of lives. This transition highlights a sobering reality. Sincerity is not a substitute for truth. A person can be deeply authentically sincere in their belief and still be fundamentally wrong in a way that cost lives. The transition from doctrine to bloodshed is perhaps most visible in the religious conflicts of Europe, such as the Thirty Years' War. What began as a confessional struggle between Catholic and Protestant powers rapidly spiraled into a broader political catastrophe that redefined the continent. This period serves as a powerful case study in how abstract theological disagreements can end as state-sanctioned violence and shifted borders. This pattern of social violence is further illustrated by the early modern witch hunts, where collective belief turned suspicion into systematic persecution. According to historical records, these hunts led to approximately a hundred thousand prosecutions and up to 60,000 executions, the vast majority of whom were women. This was not a failure of law, but a success of belief, a moment where fear, rumor, and moral certainty combined to create a lethal social environment. History is full of these moments where people don't kill because they had evidence. They killed because they had certainty. In the absence of doubt, belief becomes a license to destroy.
